title: Whites: fruit or texture
subtitle: Two paths for white wine
objectives: Compare protective and oxidative white winemaking
Explain the role of skin contact and solids

steps.title: Protective winemaking
steps.body: To keep fresh, primary fruit, winemakers work protectively: cold grapes, fast pressing, inert gas, SO2, clear juice, cool fermentation in steel. This suits aromatic varieties like Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling. The aim is purity and crispness.

steps.title: Oxidative handling
steps.body: Some winemakers let the juice brown deliberately, called hyperoxidation, so unstable compounds drop out and the wine becomes more resistant to later oxidation. Others ferment cloudier juice with more solids, which adds texture and complexity. These choices suit Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc more than aromatic grapes.

steps.prompt: Which grape is most likely to be made protectively to preserve its aromas?
steps.explanation: Sauvignon Blanc relies on fresh, volatile aromas, so it is usually handled protectively.

steps.title: Building texture
steps.body: Texture comes from several tools. Barrel fermentation adds richness. Lees contact, especially with stirring, called bâtonnage, releases compounds that add creaminess and protect against oxygen. Skin contact adds phenolics and grip. Malolactic conversion lowers acidity and rounds the wine.

steps.prompt: Which techniques add texture to a white wine?
steps.explanation: Very clear juice in steel keeps the wine crisp and pure, not textured.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Protective winemaking keeps aromatic whites fresh and pure
Oxidative handling and cloudy juice build resilience and complexity
Lees, barrels, skins and malolactic add texture
